node.title: Local Spring Boot web app, reusing the banking-app stack
node.question: Where does swe-prep run, and what is it built with?
node.decision: A local web app: Spring Boot 3.4.3 on Java 21 (Spring Web, Data JPA, Actuator, Lombok) with Postgres on the backend, React + Vite with Monaco on the front end, reusing the Team-7-Banking-Application stack. Reached over the tailnet now, with the runner behind an interface and a seeded single user (no auth) so hosting later is a deployment project rather than a rewrite.
node.why: Front-end practice requires rendering and asserting in a browser, which only a web app shape covers without a second platform; a web app's usual weakness (server not running) is answered by autostarting it as a systemd user unit, giving one-click access with no cold start; reusing the banking app's stack removes learning cost and stack-selection risk; Postgres is already configured, is the industry default and a resume keyword, and avoids a future migration; carrying a user id from day one but skipping login makes auth later roughly a day's work instead of a schema refactor, and avoids putting a login screen between the captain and his daily drill.

rejected.alternative: TUI / terminal app
rejected.why_it_lost: Would have the lowest friction for a heavy terminal user, but can never render or assert in a browser for front-end grading, so it fails domain coverage.

rejected.alternative: Desktop app
rejected.why_it_lost: Would have to embed a browser to fake front-end grading, so it does not avoid needing a second platform.

rejected.alternative: SQLite
rejected.why_it_lost: Its only advantage was needing no service, which is worth little against Postgres already being configured, used, behind JPA, and avoiding a hosting-time migration.

rejected.alternative: Building authentication now
rejected.why_it_lost: The expensive part of adding auth is discovering the schema assumed a single implicit user, not Spring Security itself; modeling the user id from the start makes it cheap later, and a login screen now would add friction to the habit the tool exists to remove.

node.soundbite: swe-prep runs as a local Spring Boot and React web app, on the banking app's stack, reached over the tailnet with no login screen.

node.title: Three-tier daily session shape
node.question: What does one daily session actually look like: how long it takes, what it contains, what happens on a wrong answer or getting stuck, and what counts as done?
node.decision: A session has three tiers, and only the first is required: a ~4-minute, ~8-rep warm-up that alone completes the day; an optional ~30-minute main exercise offered after it, whose decline still counts as a completed day; and an uncapped open continuation after that for whoever wants to keep going.
node.why: The required core has to be small enough that it is never skipped, because bad days rather than good days are what threaten the habit, and a long required minimum is a session you skip when tired, which usually ends the habit. The warm-up is not filler protecting a streak: pattern recognition is high-value-per-minute training on its own, and the main exercise is how that recognition converts into execution. Separating the required core from the rest also keeps the streak honest, since the streak measures showing up while the exercises measure improving, and conflating the two makes a single-player streak feel fake.

rejected.alternative: A required minimum session long enough to include a full problem (around 40 minutes)
rejected.why_it_lost: A 40-minute minimum is a session you skip when tired, and one skip usually ends the habit.

node.soundbite: A day is done once you finish the four-minute warm-up; everything after that is optional.

node.title: Submission judging: pass/fail correctness, opt-in failure detail, measured complexity
node.question: What does the app check when the captain hits run, and what verdicts, feedback, and history does that judging produce?
node.decision: A submission is judged pass/fail on test cases only, with no partial credit; the count of tests passed is shown but is not a score. On failure the app reports only how many tests failed, and only reveals the specific failing case (input, expected, actual) when the user explicitly asks, an action that is recorded but never penalised. After tests pass, the app asks the user to self-report their solution's time and space complexity before showing the authored target, then checks that claim by running the submission at growing input sizes and fitting the runtime curve, reporting coarse, hedged results rather than a flat correct/incorrect when measurement is inconclusive. There is no automated style feedback. Resource limits (time, memory) are reported for interest but not graded, with a generous timeout only to catch infinite loops. Every attempt is persisted, not just the final verdict, recording pass/fail, submissions taken, hint-ladder rungs climbed, whether the failing case was revealed, the complexity self-assessment, what measurement said about it, and whether the exercise was abandoned.
node.why: Partial credit would invent a number that means nothing and soften the only honest signal available. Always handing over the failing case trains debugging rather than the interview skill of reasoning about your own code without an oracle, and penalising the opt-in reveal would only teach the user to game a self-imposed system. A self-report alone would congratulate an O(n^2) solution claiming O(n), so the claim is scored against empirical measurement instead of trusted outright; measurement reliably catches polynomial blow-up but cannot cleanly separate O(n) from O(n log n), so the app must make only coarse claims. Automated style nagging is noise and not what interviews reject people over. Grading wall-clock time would punish JVM warm-up and teach nothing. Durable per-attempt records are needed because this history is the scheduler's input, and thin records would quietly cripple that ticket.

rejected.alternative: Partial credit for submissions
rejected.why_it_lost: It would invent a number that means nothing and soften the only honest signal available.

rejected.alternative: Always revealing the failing case immediately on failure
rejected.why_it_lost: It trains the opposite reflex from what a real interview tests: reasoning about your own code without an oracle.

rejected.alternative: Penalising use of the failing-case reveal
rejected.why_it_lost: Penalties on a self-imposed system only teach the user to game themselves.

rejected.alternative: Trusting the complexity self-report alone (honour-system checkbox)
rejected.why_it_lost: It would congratulate an O(n^2) solution claiming to be O(n), the single case most worth catching.

rejected.alternative: Automated style feedback
rejected.why_it_lost: Style nagging is noise and is not what interviews reject people over.

rejected.alternative: Grading on wall-clock resource limits
rejected.why_it_lost: It would punish JVM warm-up and teach nothing.

node.soundbite: A submission passes or fails on its tests alone, the failing case stays hidden until you ask for it, and a claimed time complexity is checked by measuring how the runtime actually grows rather than taking your word for it.

node.title: Split Grader from Runner, test cases as language-neutral data
node.question: How to design the exercise and runner abstraction so exercises across languages and domains (algorithms, SQL, concepts, front end) share one model without exercise secretly meaning thing that runs code.
node.decision: Split Grader (decides pass or fail) from Runner (only executes), and make test cases language-neutral JSON data rather than language-specific code, with the language adapter supplying the harness that deserialises and reserialises for the target language.
node.why: Keeping what the user produces separate from how it is judged is what stops exercise from secretly meaning code: a concept question has a Grader and no Runner at all, a Java problem and a SQL query both need a Runner but entirely different Graders, and a front-end exercise would be a different Grader over a browser Runner. Test cases as data mean a test case is authored once and runs in every language ever added, avoiding re-authoring the whole problem set for each new language.

rejected.alternative: The obvious design where Exercise directly means a thing that runs code, conflating Grader and Runner
rejected.why_it_lost: It makes concepts and warm-up reps become special cases bolted on the side afterward.

rejected.alternative: Writing test cases as JUnit (language-specific code)
rejected.why_it_lost: Every new language would require re-authoring the entire problem set, which is the difference between pluggable languages being real and being aspirational.

rejected.alternative: Inventing a new serialisation convention for trees and linked lists
rejected.why_it_lost: LeetCode's existing convention is adopted instead, since the captain will be reading their problem statements anyway.

node.title: Streak mechanic: real commit record over invented currency
node.question: What makes a single-player streak actually stick, given that the captain is the only user and the only author, and can edit the database and turn off any nag he writes?
node.decision: Cut invented currency entirely (no XP, no hearts, no lives, no leagues). Instead: commit real solved problems to a private repo with private contributions counted on the GitHub profile, so the contribution graph becomes a true external record; show a true readiness picture (patterns covered, what is shaky, what has not been touched, cold-solve rate) computed from existing attempt records instead of a score; add a scheduled notification cue at a chosen time so the decision to practise is not made fresh each day; display days practised as a non-spendable record shown next to readiness; and allow a missed day to be repaired by a double session the next day, capped at roughly two per month.
node.why: Duolingo's streak mechanics depend on other people, leagues, loss aversion against a public record, and notifications from a party that is not the user, none of which swe-prep has. The captain is both the only user and the author, he knows any points are invented, and he can edit the database, so a self-printed number is one he stops believing in around week two and a fake number going up actively misleads him about whether he is getting hired. The design instead removes every excuse, makes the record true rather than invented, and makes breaking it cost something real.

rejected.alternative: Invented currency (XP, hearts, lives, leagues)
rejected.why_it_lost: Any number the captain can print himself is a number he stops believing in around week two, and a fake number that goes up is actively misleading about whether he is getting hired.

rejected.alternative: Publishing the solved solutions publicly
rejected.why_it_lost: The captain declined, and a public dump of solutions reads as interview grinding rather than building, plus it would collide with the licensing question if statements ride along with the solutions.

rejected.alternative: Financial stakes (Beeminder-style)
rejected.why_it_lost: They genuinely work, but wiring up money is real friction, and adding a punishment to an activity already being avoided is more likely to increase the avoidance than fix it. Left available later if nothing else lands.

node.soundbite: The streak sticks through a real private-repo commit record, an honest readiness picture, a scheduled cue, and a capped repair mechanic, not invented points.

node.title: Two schedulers over one shared record: due-date reps, priority-score challenges
node.question: How does the app choose what the captain practises next - specifically whether spaced-repetition intervals built for flashcards survive a 30-40 minute problem, and what happens with a never-seen problem versus one failed twice versus one passed cleanly three times
node.decision: Use two separate schedulers over one shared record rather than one selection model: a due-date queue running standard spaced repetition (SM-2, kept swappable) for reps, and a daily priority score for challenges that picks the single highest-scoring problem rather than working off a due date
node.why: Spaced repetition assumes reviews are cheap, which holds for reps (seconds each, so twenty due costs four minutes) but breaks for a 30-40 minute challenge, where twenty due is a fortnight of work and a scheduler generating that debt gets ignored within a week. The scarcity is also structural: roughly 90 challenge slots exist in three months against about 75 problems, leaving barely room for one pass, so the scheduler must respect that rather than pretend otherwise. A due date asks what is owed; a priority score asks what is worth it, and only the second survives that scarcity.

rejected.alternative: One scheduler serving both reps and challenges
rejected.why_it_lost: The cheap-review arithmetic spaced repetition depends on does not hold once a review costs 30-40 minutes instead of seconds, and the challenge slot scarcity is structural, not a detail a shared model could absorb

rejected.alternative: FSRS instead of SM-2 for the rep queue
rejected.why_it_lost: FSRS is better on paper, but the record states the difference is marginal at the scale of one user and roughly 400 reps, so the algorithm is kept swappable rather than agonised over

rejected.alternative: Feeding the judging ticket's raw per-attempt fields directly into the scheduling algorithms
rejected.why_it_lost: Collapsing into a single 0-5 quality score instead keeps the scheduler from ossifying around today's exact set of recorded fields

rejected.alternative: Using time taken as a scheduling signal
rejected.why_it_lost: Deliberately excluded as noise - interruptions, thinking before typing, and typing fast on a misunderstood problem all corrupt it, adding variance without carrying information

rejected.alternative: Unbounded introduction of new problems (Anki's failure mode)
rejected.why_it_lost: Unbounded new material lets review debt pile up until the user quits, so the resolution orders review debt first, new problems second, with a weekly cap on introductions

rejected.alternative: Deleting problems once mastered
rejected.why_it_lost: Nothing is ever deleted - a problem passed cleanly three times earns a months-long interval, which the record calls retirement, not removal

node.soundbite: Reps are pulled from a due-date spaced-repetition queue because reviews are cheap, and challenges are picked by a daily priority score because slots are scarce and a due date alone cannot tell you what's worth forty minutes today.

node.question: What is a warm-up rep, concretely, in each domain, and how are they authored?

node.title: SQL exercise engine, fixtures, and grading
node.question: What does a SQL exercise actually look like - which engine it runs against, how fixtures are shared across exercises, how results are compared, what topics and how many exercises are covered, what a SQL warm-up rep is, and whether a complexity or query-plan target applies?
node.decision: SQL exercises run against the same Postgres instance as the app, but on a separate fixture database, with each attempt isolated by a transaction that is rolled back and a submission connection restricted to a read-only role. Fixtures are two or three shared, realistic schemas (e.g. an e-commerce schema and an events/analytics schema) with many exercises authored against each, rather than one schema per exercise. Result comparison treats the result set as a multiset of rows, matching columns by position and ignoring column names, respecting row order only when the exercise explicitly asked for it, with a normalisation pass for numeric types, float rounding, and NULLs. Failure is reported minimally (expected vs. actual row count) under the withhold-by-default judging rule, with the full diff available on request. Roughly 25-40 exercises cover joins, aggregation/GROUP BY/HAVING, subqueries and CTEs, window functions, NULL semantics, duplicates, date bucketing, and top-N-per-group. SQL warm-up reps reuse the five rep types from the warm-up rep decision, substituting predict-the-output for the complexity slot, with spot-the-bug called out as the standout type, all derived from the same reference query used for the graded exercise. SQL exercises carry no complexity target, and query plans are deferred rather than built.
node.why: Dialect parity is the deciding factor for the engine: SQLite or H2 would be easier to embed but would train on the wrong dialect (window function syntax, FULL OUTER JOIN, and type handling all differ from Postgres, which is what the captain will actually interview on), and Postgres is already running for app state so there is no new infrastructure to add. Per-attempt transaction rollback gives perfect isolation at zero cost and handles exercises that write as well as those that only read. A shared schema is learned once and then answers many questions, which is how real SQL interviews and the job itself work, and it is also what makes a seconds-long SQL warm-up rep viable at all - per-exercise fixtures would burn a 30-minute budget re-reading an unfamiliar schema. Comparing results as a multiset while ignoring column names avoids failing the captain over a cosmetic alias, while matching by position still holds him to the asked column order; a normalisation pass is required for numeric types, float rounding, and NULL handling or false failures would be constant. Query plans are deferred because they are shallow at entry level and grading on EXPLAIN output is a research project rather than a feature.

rejected.alternative: An embedded engine such as SQLite or H2 for exercise fixtures
rejected.why_it_lost: It would be easier to embed but would train the captain on a dialect he will not interview in - window function syntax, FULL OUTER JOIN, and type handling all differ from Postgres in ways that bite in a real interview.

rejected.alternative: Per-exercise fixtures, authored separately for each exercise
rejected.why_it_lost: They sound cleaner but are worse in practice - most of a 30-minute budget would go on re-reading an unfamiliar schema instead of writing SQL, and they would make SQL warm-up reps impractical.

rejected.alternative: Grading SQL exercises against EXPLAIN/query-plan output
rejected.why_it_lost: Query plans are a real interview topic but shallow at entry level, and grading on EXPLAIN output is a research project rather than a feature; if it ever happens it belongs as a rep type, not a graded exercise.

node.soundbite: SQL exercises run against a Postgres fixture database rolled back per attempt on a shared realistic schema, and grade by comparing result rows as an unordered multiset.
